newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Half-hearted response to S.Korean strike call.
newsitem.headline: Half-hearted response to S.Korean strike call.

text.p: South Korean workers gave a half-hearted response on Wednesday to a strike call by an outlawed union group following President Kim Young-sam's stunning retreat over a controversial labour law.

Police picked up a fugitive leader from the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions but later released him in line with Kim's new spirit of compromise over the law, which he said on Tuesday could be sent back to parliament for debate.
Dan Byong-ho was one of seven confederation leaders holed up at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral. He was detained for two hours of questioning near the capital, a state prosecutor said.

Police have withdrawn from the church following Kim's order to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders, although it was unclear how long other confederation heads would stay in a ramshackle tent on the cathedral grounds.
Stocks fell sharply on fears that Kim's reversal would delay restructuring of the economy, brokers said. The main index fell 16.87 points, or 2.44 percent, to 673.67 by the morning close.

The Labour Ministry said it expected 68,500 workers from the 12-million strong workforce to strike over the law, which allows firms to sack workers and replace strikers. It said this would mainly be confined to the automobile industry.

The confederation said in a statement that about 150,000 workers were expected to observe the call. It said the government must scrap the law, forced through parliament late last year, and come up with a new bill before March 1.
The statement repeated the union's threat to call out all its 500,000 members for an indefinite strike from February 18 if the law was not repealed.
President Kim's dramatic climbdown followed a decision by the confederation to call off indefinite stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week.
In a major concession to the opposition, Kim conceded that forced passage of the law had caused public anxiety and damaged the economy, and agreed to send it back to parliament.
Political analysts have also said Kim was bowing to public criticism over the forced passage of the law, with many commentators comparing his tactics to those of previous military rulers.
But Kim, who said the strife had defeated the law's aim of revitalising the economy, insisted dumping the legislation would go against the constitution and that it could only be revised.
He has said the law was needed to free up the labour market, thus trimming corporate costs and boosting competitiveness.
A Hyundai Motor Co Ltd union official in the southeast city of Ulsan said 29,000 confederation members had joined the strike and that production would be halted for one day.
But Lee Chung-tak, a company public relations officer, said although production was slow, the factory was still running.
"About 30 percent of management, or white collar labourers, have joined the production lines," Lee told Reuters.
A union official from Ulsan-based Hyundai Heavy Industries, the nation's largest shipyard, said only 210 workers had joined the stoppages. Production would not be affected, he said.
Union members at automaker Kia Motors, located just outside Seoul, would hold partial strikes for four hours in the afternoon, a confederation union official said.
At a meeting of the heads of three main political parties on Tuesday, Kim expressed sorrow for the loss of billions of dollars in output through strikes sparked by the law.
He also agreed to reopen debate on another controversial law reviving a once notorious domestic spy agency.
According to an account of the talks by opposition leader Kim Dae-jung of the National Congress for New Politics, President Kim indicated the confederation should be recognised.
Multiple trade union representation is a major demand of international labour organisations.
The Dong-A Ilbo newspaper, a leading daily, said in an editorial it regreted failure to achieve a clear breakthrough.
"We cannot help but chide the lack of political ability of the president and the two opposition leaders," it said.
